name: Memory & bandwidth (HBM)
summary: How fast data reaches the chip often limits AI speed more than the chip's raw arithmetic.

D1.guide: Watch the narrow door. Does a faster cook help if ingredients arrive slowly?
text: Imagine a super-fast cook who has to wait for ingredients to come through a narrow door. The cook's speed doesn't matter if the door is slow.
For AI, the ingredients are the model's numbers, and the door is memory bandwidth.
D1.analogy: A fast cook waiting at a narrow pantry door.

text: Generating each token means reading the model's active weights from memory. If those weights take tens of gigabytes, every new token moves that much data. On a home machine, whether those weights fit in fast memory at all is the first question (see [local AI hardware](#/concept/local-ai-hardware)).
High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacks memory chips right next to the processor so data moves far faster than with ordinary memory.
Rule of thumb for a single user: tokens per second is roughly memory bandwidth divided by the bytes of weights read per token.
D2.analogy: A narrow door between the pantry and the kitchen.
D2.analogyBreaks: A pantry door moves each ingredient once. A model's weights are re-read for every single token, so the same data crosses the 'door' over and over; batching many users shares each trip.

predict.question: You halve the size of a model's weights (16-bit to 8-bit) on the same hardware. Roughly what happens to single-user generation speed?
predict.explanation: If generation is limited by memory reads, moving half as many bytes per token roughly doubles tokens per second; in practice a bit less.

text: To write each new token for one user, the chip has to read every weight of the model from memory once. So the speed limit is simple: **tokens per second ≤ memory bandwidth ÷ bytes read per token**.
Change the model size, the bytes per weight and the bandwidth. Then turn the compute up and down and watch what happens.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative numbers, not measured. Generic model sizes and a made-up accelerator, not real products. The bound counts weight reads only; real speeds are lower.

tasks: With the 8B model in 16-bit, double the bandwidth. What happens to the upper bound?
Now move the compute slider all the way down and back up. Does the answer change?
Switch to 4-bit weights. Why does the bound go up even though the chip is the same?

predict.question: An 8B model in 16-bit runs on memory with 800 GB/s, giving an upper bound of 50 tokens per second for one user. If you double the compute, what happens to that bound?
predict.explanation: Each token needs 16 GB of weights read from memory, and 800 GB/s can only deliver that 50 times a second. The compute was already waiting on memory, so more of it does not help.

text: A **roofline chart** asks one question: how much work does the chip do for each byte it reads? That ratio is the **arithmetic intensity**, in FLOPs per byte.
Below the **ridge point** (peak compute ÷ bandwidth) the chip is memory-bound and speed follows the bandwidth slope. Above it, the chip is compute-bound and speed hits the flat compute roof.

Generating for one user does about 2 FLOPs per weight but reads the whole weight, so intensity is tiny. Serving many users in a batch reuses each weight read for every user, which moves the point right.

interactiveConfig.note: Illustrative numbers, not measured. Generic model sizes and a made-up accelerator, not real products. Counts weight reads only (no KV cache), so these are upper bounds from the formula.

tasks: Start at batch 1 and move the batch slider up. At which batch size does the dot reach the roof?
Switch from 16-bit to 8-bit weights. Why does the ridge now arrive at half the batch size?
Double the compute. Which batch sizes get faster, and which do not change at all?
D4.code:
flops_per_step = 2 * params * batch          # multiply and add for every weight, per user
bytes_per_step = params * bytes_per_weight    # weights read once and shared by the batch
intensity = flops_per_step / bytes_per_step   # = 2 * batch / bytes_per_weight
ridge = peak_flops / bandwidth
speed = min(peak_flops, bandwidth * intensity)
total_tokens_per_s = speed / (2 * params)
per_user_tokens_per_s = total_tokens_per_s / batch
tradeoffs: Bigger batches use the chip better but each user waits for the whole batch's step.
Lower-precision weights raise intensity and speed, at some cost in accuracy.
The KV cache adds memory reads that grow with context, so real serving reaches the roof later than this chart shows.
Faster memory helps memory-bound work; more compute only helps work that is already past the ridge.

predict.question: With 16-bit weights, compute of 1,000 TFLOPS and bandwidth of 2 TB/s, the ridge is at 500 FLOPs per byte. About what batch size makes generation compute-bound?
predict.explanation: Intensity is 2 × batch ÷ 2 bytes, which equals the batch size. It reaches the ridge of 500 at a batch of about 500.

text: Where it's heading: faster HBM generations, designs with much more on-chip memory, and algorithmic tricks such as speculative decoding that get more tokens out of each memory read.

sources.title: Roofline: an insightful visual performance model (Williams, Waterman, Patterson)
